event: Black Monday: no single piece of news that day; selling had built up over the week before and automatic selling programs (portfolio insurance) fed on the fall.
First trading day after the national bank holiday: the Emergency Banking Act had passed on 9 March and most banks had reopened.
Traders expected President Hoover to announce a plan to support weak banks; the plan itself was only made public the next day.
Covid-19 fears: the Federal Reserve's emergency cut of interest rates to near zero the day before did not calm investors, and the president said a recession was possible.
First day of the 1929 crash: panic selling with no specific news event named for the day.
Black Tuesday: the panic selling went on for a second day, again with no specific news event named.
A bounce after the two crash days; John D. Rockefeller said in public that prices had fallen too far and that he was buying shares.
Congress was close to agreeing a 2 trillion dollar Covid-19 rescue package.
Covid-19: a ban on travel from Europe had been announced the evening before, and the European Central Bank did not cut interest rates as investors had hoped.
Governments in the US and Europe announced plans to put public money into their banks during the financial crisis.
Selling started again in the weeks after the October crash; the sources name no news event for the day.
Bargain hunting after weeks of heavy falls, helped by hopes that the Federal Reserve would cut interest rates.
Second day of the bounce after Black Monday: investors and companies bought shares at the lower prices while interest rates fell.
The Produce Exchange Trust Company of New York stopped paying depositors that day, and the cost of borrowing overnight on Wall Street shot up.
Word spread that General Motors would keep paying its dividend and that the Farm Board had sold its wheat; traders who had bet on falls rushed to buy back.
Rumours that the Federal Reserve would be allowed to lend more freely, as Congress took up a banking bill (the Glass-Steagall Act of 1932).
The president declared a national emergency over Covid-19, releasing 50 billion dollars; this came one day after a 10% fall.
The slide that began in October had reached its low the day before; this was the first day of the recovery, and the source names no news for it.
